_doc: Rewilding sites (world/rewild.gd). Each site is a rectangle [x, y, w, h] of an existing zone, restored in four stages: 0 Damaged, 1 Planted, 2 Recovering, 3 Wild. tasks[i] takes the site from stage i to i+1 (kinds: plant, litter, items, money, show, battle). Stage 1 comes at once; stages 2 and 3 settle over one in-game day. rewards[i] runs as story commands when stage i+1 is reached. encounters[i] join the zone's table from stage i+1 (requires_flag rewild_<site>). looks: biome -> four stage looks (ground colours, tall grass, lattice blockers, decor meshes).

tasks.ask: Here, take a bucket of sphagnum plugs. I've marked five spots with canes. Push one in at each, like you're tucking in a very wet baby.
Next we block the gullies so the water stays put. Wool bales work a treat. Bring me 3 Sheep Wool, off the fences, mind, not off the sheep.
One problem. There's an Enclosure lad up top still cutting drains. Nobody told him they've gone bust. Will you go and tell him? Firmly?

intro: Ey up, me duck. Mind where you put your feet, it's not so much a moor as a very big scab.
The Enclosure drained this lot for grouse and grazing. Peat dries out, peat blows away, and down in Stockport they wonder why the river comes up brown.
I'm Hilda. Me and the volunteers are putting it back. Fancy getting your boots mucky?
stages: Bare peat, gullies like a ploughed field and a drainpipe where a bog should be. Breaks your heart.
Look at that! Green coming through. The sphagnum's taken, and it's holding water like a sponge holds a grudge.
Pools! Proper bog pools! I nearly cried. I did cry, actually. Don't tell the volunteers.
Cotton grass nodding, bog pools full and the water voles are back in the cuts. Listen. You can hear the moor breathing.
lines.settling: Now we wait. Moss doesn't do next-day delivery. Give it a day and come and look.
done: That's done it. Look at it, settling in like it owns the place.
Hear that? Something's come back. The moor's telling everyone.
lines.wild: You've made an old woman very happy and a moor very soggy. Come back whenever. Bring a flask.

tasks.ask: There's five canes in the brash. Each one wants a sessile oak, a proper Welsh one, not one of those flashy English ones. Off you go, bach.
Now the deer will have those saplings for breakfast unless we guard them. Tree guards cost money, and the Enclosure left us a debt and a dead fern. Could you spare 800?
Last thing. A wood's not a wood without its night shift. Bring me a Night creature and let it have a sniff round, so the others know it's safe. It stays with you, don't worry, I'm not running a zoo.

intro: Duw, mind the brash. The Enclosure clear-felled their spruce here and left the stumps like a mouthful of bad teeth.
This used to be rainforest. Yes, in Wales. Mossy oaks, ferns on the branches, lichen like old lace. It rains enough, God knows.
I'm Gwen. I'm growing it back, one oak at a time. You look like you've got hands.
stages: Stumps, brash and mud. Not a fern in sight.
Saplings in! Little things, aren't they? Like a row of nervous children on the first day of school.
Look at them now, shoulder high and cheeky with it. The ferns are coming back underneath.
Moss on every branch, ferns dripping, and a pine marten looked me in the eye this morning. Cheek of it. Lovely.
lines.settling: Give it a day, cariad. Trees aren't in a hurry. They've got a few hundred years.
done: There we are. Iawn. Lovely job.
Something new in the wood. I heard it before I saw it.
lines.wild: Coed Padarn, as it should be. Come and get rained on under it any time.

tasks.ask: Trouble is, there's an Enclosure stalker still keeping the deer numbers up for the shooting. Too many deer, no wee trees. Could you have a word? A battling sort of word?
Now he's away, we can plant. Five canes out there, five wee Scots pines. Seeds from the granny pines, so they're family.
A pinewood needs its rowans for the birds. Bring me 4 Rowan Berries and the thrushes will do the rest. They're very reliable, for thrushes.

intro: Aye, it's a bonny glen. Bonny like a putting green. That's the trouble.
Every seedling that pokes its head up gets eaten by a deer or a sheep before it's said good morning. The old pines are all grannies now, and they've no grandweans.
I'm Morag. We're bringing the Caledonian forest back to Dundreggan. Will you lend a hand?
stages: Grass cropped to the bone, and not a young tree in the glen.
Seedlings in, guards on. They're wee, but they're thrawn.
Young pines up to your shoulder, heather coming in between. It's starting to smell like a forest.
Pinewood. Juniper and blaeberry, and a capercaillie clattering about like a dropped tea tray. Magic.
lines.settling: Give it a day. A pine takes its time, and so should we.
done: There now. That's taken. You can see it, can't you?
Did you hear that in the trees? Something's moved back in.
lines.wild: You've given the glen its grandweans back. Come and sit under them when they're tall.

tasks.ask: First job's the rubbish. There's five piles along the bank. Bag them up and mind the trolley, it bites.
Now, the river creatures want to know it's safe. Bring us a Brook creature to have a paddle. It stays with you, I'm only borrowing its opinion.
Last of it. There's a fella with an Enclosure net strung right across the river, after the salmon. Away and sort him out, would you?

intro: Bout ye. Wee bit of a mess, so it is.
The Enclosure straightened the Bush and dumped half of Coleraine in it. Trolleys, tyres, a settee. A whole settee! Somebody must have been comfy.
I'm Ciaran. I'm getting the river back. You look like you don't mind wet feet.
stages: Litter in the reeds, litter in the river, litter in places I'd rather not think about.
Clean as a whistle, and the willow whips are in. The water's running clearer already.
Reeds coming thick along the bank, and somebody's started building a dam. Somebody with very big teeth.
Reedbed, beaver dam, salmon in the pools. And at dusk there's a boom out of the reeds like someone blowing over a milk bottle. A bittern! In Bushmills!
lines.settling: Leave it a day. The river knows what it's doing once you stop throwing settees in it.
done: Did you see that? Something's back on the river. Don't scare it.
lines.wild: That's the Bush running wild again. You're a legend, so you are. Pint's on me. Lemonade, if you're driving.

tasks.ask: Before we start, show me a Bog creature, would you? If it likes the place we know where to begin. Sure, it stays with you. I've three cats and a husband, I've no room.
The drains have to be blocked so the water comes back up. Peat dams don't build themselves and the digger man wants paying. Could you put 600 towards it?
Now the fun bit. Five canes out on the cutaway. Plant a sphagnum plug at each and the bog will do the rest. Bogs are very good at the rest.

intro: God, you're very welcome. Mind the drains, they're deeper than they look and so is my opinion of the Enclosure.
They milled this bog flat for turf and left it bare as a car park. A bog's a sponge, you know. This one's been wrung out.
I'm Brid. We're wetting it back up. Are you any good at getting muddy?
stages: Bare cutaway and straight black drains. Not a bit of life in it.
The drains are blocked and the water's coming up. You can see the shine on it now.
Pools, and the bog cotton's out. My heart's lepping.
Wet, wild and full of life. The cranes came back last week. Cranes! Nesting in Connemara! I rang my mother.
lines.settling: Give it a day now. A bog takes a thousand years to make, so a day's nothing.
done: That's grand. That's more than grand.
Did you hear that? There's something new out on the bog.
lines.wild: You've done a lovely thing here. Come back in a thousand years and see how it's getting on.

tasks.ask: First, the rubbish. Five heaps along the broogh. Bag them up and I'll fetch the barrow.
Now we plant a sod hedge, the Manx way. Hawthorn for the top. Bring me 3 Hawthorn Berries and I'll grow the rest myself. Eventually.
The birds need telling it's safe to come back. Bring a Gale creature for a fly about. It stays with you, it's a recommendation, not a donation.

intro: Moghrey mie! That's good morning. It's not a good morning for the broogh, mind.
This bank by the railway was all gorse and heather once. The Enclosure scraped it bare for a car park nobody ever built, and the choughs went off in a huff.
I'm Juan. Traa dy liooar, we say. Time enough. But I'd still like a hand.
stages: Scraped earth and tyre ruts. A broogh with nothing on it but a bad mood.
Clean, and the first gorse is in. It's small, but it's already prickly. That's Manx for you.
Heather and gorse coming up together, and the choughs are back on the chimneys.
Gorse in flower, heather humming with bees, and the puffins have come round from the Calf to see what the fuss is. Smells like coconut now, gorse does.
lines.settling: Traa dy liooar. Give it a day.
done: Look up! Something's come back to the broogh.
lines.wild: That's the broogh wild again. Even the wind seems happier. Well. Slightly.
